|---|---|---|

   - Uses a **single panel** (no faceting or small multiples).

   - Categories are arranged as a **ranked list** of occupations.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / job title | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Difference from original projection (%) | Quantitative | Bar length; horizontal position relative to central zero line; numeric labels |
| Direction of change (positive vs. negative) | Categorical/nominal (derived sign) | Side of the zero line (left for negative, right for positive) |
| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |

A catchy headline for this graph could be "How will our jobs be affected in the coming years as a result of Covid-19?"

raw_comment:
Off the bat, the most noticeable thing when looking at the lists of jobs is the obvious divide between STEM jobs, and service jobs. All jobs on the top half section of the graph show massive increases, whereas the lower half will be experiencing major decreases. I have mixed feelings when I see statistics like this, since I understand not all workers desire to pursue STEM careers. Service jobs are essentially the backbone of modern society, and this decline in them can only mean one thing, and that it is not the jobs that are going away, but the people who perform them. Throughout the pandemic we have all noticed how quick companies were to adjust the function of their services to allow for business to thrive while following CDC guidelines. Where a lot of companies turned to computers and robots to perform tasks normally done by humans. Many of the service jobs on the list consist precisely of those jobs I have seen done by a computer at least once. Knowledge intensive jobs such as the ones on the top half of the graph are very encouraging to see, as they mean our society is progressing rapidly in terms of knowledge and technology. Though I can’t help but feel pity for those who had passions in their jobs which appeared “replaceable” to many companies. 

Headline : “ Service jobs on a decline, start getting those STEM degrees”

A catchy headline for this graph could be: How will the Pandemic Impact Your Future Job?

   - Categories are arranged as a **ranked list** of occupations.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / job title | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Difference from original projection (%) | Quantitative | Bar length; horizontal position relative to central zero line; numeric labels |
| Direction of change (positive vs. negative) | Categorical/nominal (derived sign) | Side of the zero line (left for negative, right for positive) |
| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |
raw_comment:
When I first viewed this graph, I immediately noticed that a wide variety of careers related to the field of science appeared to have increased in demand. I wonder whether this occurred due to the fact that most of these careers contribute to reducing the effect of the widespread pandemic we are currently living in. For example, epidemiologists seem to be higher in demand than all of the careers depicted on the graph because they are tasked with identifying patterns and causes of disease. Furthermore, I also noticed that careers in relation to customer service such as bartenders or waiters/waitresses seemed to have decreased in demand.

This could either adversely or positively affect my community since I myself have both medical professionals in my neighborhood and family who would benefit from the effects of the pandemic, as well as people working in customer service who are no longer needed as much since there are less people going out in public places than ever before.

One possible title for this graph could be "How Has the Pandemic Impacted Your Career?" since the graph shows an array of jobs that the audience may have themselves, or may know of someone who works in one of these fields as well.

Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs: “Impact of the Deadly Virus on Jobs: How Does It Impact YOU?” by Mia of Washington, “Is Your Job Safe?: Career Demand After the Pandemic” by Grace, Kaitlin, Evan, Brian of Eden Prairie High School in Minnesota, “Pandemic Pandemonium Will Shift the Future of Our Job Market” by Will of Dallas and "How Secure is Your Future Career Going to Be Post-Pandemic?" by Christina and "The New Occupational Crisis" by William, both from Long Island in New York.

1. **Chart type**  
   Diverging horizontal bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **single panel** (no faceting or small multiples).
   - Bars **diverge from a central vertical baseline** at 0, with positive values extending right and negative values extending left.
   - Categories are arranged as a **ranked list** of occupations.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / job title | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Difference from original projection (%) | Quantitative | Bar length; horizontal position relative to central zero line; numeric labels |
| Direction of change (positive vs. negative) | Categorical/nominal (derived sign) | Side of the zero line (left for negative, right for positive) |
| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |

I noticed is that the bar graph shows many different jobs and how they were positively or negatively affected by the pandemic through percentages.The jobs which percentages are increasing are mostly related to technological and medical fields. While the jobs which the percentages are decreasing, are jobs relating to everyday service to many people such as waiters, cashiers, bartenders, etc.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that almost all the jobs that are impacted negatively by the pandemic are service jobs while almost all the jobs that are impacted positively by the pandemic are jobs based in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics). The job that is impacted most positively is epidemiologists. The job that is impacted most negatively is bus drivers. Neither of these statistics are surprising. Epidemiologists are needed significantly right now in order to devise ways to remedy the impacts and spread of the pandemic. However, bus drivers are needed less and less as schools turn virtual and people fear catching COVID-19 on public transportation.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how long these impacts on the job market might last. Will they last just until the pandemic is under control? Will they last for a few years after the pandemic? Will they last for decades?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Myself and many of my peers are entering college with the intention of major in STEM. Some are majoring in biochemistry, some are majoring in computer science, and some are majoring in biology. If the data in this graph is to have lasting impacts, the pandemic will have a positive effect on my own and my peers' job prospects. If STEM careers are gaining popularity due to the pandemic, it will make it much easier to find jobs that relate to STEM majors. 

Headline: Has the pandemic stolen your job?

It's also shown how much our society relies on technology and the internet now, as it's helping many of us attend school, work from home, etc.

I wonder what will happen to the people who are working/planning to work in industries that are predicted to have a decrease in demand. Can their current skills be used in the technology/medical field or will they have to attend school or obtain some sort of training to find a more stable job?

But for my community, this may mean a lot of people losing their jobs and being forced to learn new skills to keep up with the jobs needed in our technologically advanced world.

For a headline I think a good one could be: The Future of Our Jobs: The Pandemic Decides. While these predicted trends aren't only based off of the pandemic, it's heavily influenced by it.

Greetings everyone!  

I am Moderator Bill, a high school math teacher in Collinsville, IL.  I will be taking over moderating duties from the fantastic Moderator Sharon.  

I wanted to share my thoughts with this graph as I start reviewing and responding to other's comments.  

The obvious thing to notice is that specific science and technology jobs are projected to have larger projected positive job growths over the next 10 years while service industry jobs are projected to have a negative growth over the same time period.  These projected changes are what they say they are: projected, meaning it is not a guaranteed thing to occur, but, based on mathematical models using current data, could possibly happen, especially in using this "strong-impact scenario".   We should always consider key words in reports, like in this story: "How MIGHT....", to realize that, again, these are just projected numbers.  Things can easily change for the better or for the worse over the next ten years.

I believe this information gives students still in school some insight into potential areas of future studies if they want to have more job security later in life.  The article that includes this graph mentions that 75% of all employment sectors are projected to change by less than 2%, so the jobs we see here only represent a small portion of the largest projected changes.

raw_comment: The first thing I notice is the large increase in scientific and medical fields while there is a decrease to more interpersonal and hospitality based occupations. I wonder if this is permanent or even a possibility anymore with increased vaccination numbers and the steps towards better, treatment, immunity and care. I doubt, given the fact that the world is slowly getting back to normal, that these changes will actually last into the next couple years. However, I wonder how the culture and priorities of the people post-pandemic will affect these fields in the coming years. I also wonder if businesses, especially smaller, more local businesses that struggled or even closed down will be able to recover, having personally seen multiple new businesses have to close down during the harder times of the pandemic. While the decrease in more interpersonal jobs is definitely a bad sign right now, I have optimism that in the coming years, as the world returns to normal, these reductions only mean that there will be more job opportunities for the incoming working class of the future.

raw_comment:
“Post Pandemic vs Occupations”

After analyzing the graph we noticed that there will be a much greater demand for epidemiologists because they deal with the distribution and control of diseases that could help prevent another pandemic. Science-related fields show the biggest increase in demand post-pandemic. There is more of an overall decrease for certain jobs since they require being surrounded by people in an indoor setting. Public transit-related jobs show a significant decrease because fewer people will feel safe in those situations. We had some questions about the graph such as if the jobs that are currently in low demand will come back after the pandemic if they may go out of business. We wonder if the jobs that are in low demand, such as a restaurant host and a cashier, will be replaced with technology or robots someday. We also wonder if the small businesses that were struggling will be able to thrive after the pandemic is over. This impacts our community because it makes it harder to get jobs that do not require a lot of training or education. This leaves people in our community unemployed and struggling with finances. Also, Those who can’t afford a high education rely on cashier or waitress jobs, but these jobs are in low demand right now.

1. **Chart type**  
   Diverging horizontal bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **single panel** (no faceting or small multiples).
   - Bars **diverge from a central vertical baseline** at 0, with positive values extending right and negative values extending left.
   - Categories are arranged as a **ranked list** of occupations.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / job title | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Difference from original projection (%) | Quantitative | Bar length; horizontal position relative to central zero line; numeric labels |
| Direction of change (positive vs. negative) | Categorical/nominal (derived sign) | Side of the zero line (left for negative, right for positive) |
| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |
raw_comment:
Based on the projections presented in this graph, our group found that jobs relating to the medical field have significantly gone up in demand as a result of the pandemic. The demand for workers in service sectors, including flight attendants, waiters and waitresses, and cashiers, has gone down significantly. Based on this data, we wonder, once the economy opens up, will the need for technology based companies decrease, or remain the same? Has Covid-19 heightened our need for communication via the internet? Additionally, how have the projections compared to what has actually happened? Lastly, we wonder if businesses will continue to proceed with any adaptations made to job demand even after the pandemic is long gone? The impact this change of demand has is that some groups of professions are losing jobs while others are hiring more. Because of the sudden loss of jobs, the economy declined. This decline in certain job markets has the potential to destabilize the economy and hurt many working class families.

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s bar chart shows the largest projected percentage changes, both negatively and positively, in the number of jobs by employment sector for the period from 2019 to 2029.  This change is due, in part, to the effects of the pandemic on the U.S. economy’s long-term, job trends.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this bar chart. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this bar chart and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next graph on Covid-19 in prisons will be released by Friday, April 30 with moderation on Wednesday, May 5.

raw_comment:
Upon looking at the graph I wonder one thing and notice two others:
1. I wonder how the future of the entertainment industry will be impacted after this pandemic
2. I noticed that there was a spike in the number of epidemiologists and other medical practitioners, which makes sense given what happened during the pandemic
3. I noticed and am a bit shocked by the low increase in the predicted demand for microbiologists, I would have thought that there would be a much greater increase given that that field of study ties into viruses and how they interact with other organisms.

1. **Chart type**  
   Diverging horizontal bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **single panel** (no faceting or small multiples).
   - Bars **diverge from a central vertical baseline** at 0, with positive values extending right and negative values extending left.
   - Categories are arranged as a **ranked list** of occupations.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / job title | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Difference from original projection (%) | Quantitative | Bar length; horizontal position relative to central zero line; numeric labels |
| Direction of change (positive vs. negative) | Categorical/nominal (derived sign) | Side of the zero line (left for negative, right for positive) |
| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |
raw_comment: I notice that this is a graph regarding how future jobs might be impacted as a result of the current Coronavirus pandemic. I can see that the highest increase is in epidemiology, which makes sense because we are in a pandemic. The increased jobs that come after it are also in the medical field, biochemistry, and data analyzers, and biomedical technicians. I can see that what might decrease over time are jobs in retail, restaurants, and other in-person jobs. I wonder as to why it is that we see this trend. My assumptions are that the current pandemic really took a toll on how we are living now -- it has become the norm that people stay at home and work in addition to students learning from home as well. This narrative defeats the purpose of having office buildings and schools because what was once done in person can be also done at home. This reasoning might be the reason why we see these trends. The impact that this has on me and my community is that it makes it a lot harder to look towards a positive and pre-covid future because of how long we've been in a pandemic. I feel like in my community we might start seeing less people working in offices when the same jobs can be done at home. Maybe in schools, a lot of programs will be done online to eliminate the struggle of finding buildings and providing necessities. Catchy headline: "What Jobs Might Look Like Post-Pandemic".

I noticed that jobs related to STEM have surged in the strong impact scenario while jobs in the service sector have greatly fallen. The general trend appears to follow the COVID health guidelines. For example, the CDC doesn't recommend travel for recreation right now, which explains why the reservation and transportation ticket agents and travel checks industry has negative job loss instead of growth. I wonder how dependant this perspective data is on COVID restrictions. For instance, if the future is not reflective of a strong impact scenario, will cashiers still have a similar percent of job loss caused by something else, like businesses preferring technology (self-checkouts) because of preferable costs? This will impact the composition of jobs among industries that make up the job market in totality. For example, if there are fewer available employment opportunities for bartenders those individuals will have to find a job in another industry. This could have an interesting impact on educational attainment levels. Individuals who were bartenders but are now unemployed may choose to go to school to become web developers or database administrators. This could have an interesting secondary impact on political demographics, as education level is a primary indicator of voting behavior. 
Catchy Headline: "Back to the Future: will the job market ever recover?"

| Rank/order of occupations | Ordinal | Vertical order of bars |
